# OtterFlop Specification

## Overview

OtterFlop is a non-commercial bedtime care game for a 4-year-old, delivered as a static web app that runs well on an Amazon Fire tablet and can be hosted for free on GitHub Pages. The deployed target is the GitHub Pages project site at `/OtterFlop/`, so the app and all assets must work correctly from that base path. The player cares for cute otter kids one at a time through a calm nightly routine: feed them, dress them with interchangeable clothing items, brush their teeth, play the Otter Flop catching game with dad, observe a visual family prayer moment, hear an instrumental lullaby from mommy otter, and tuck them into bed. The game starts with one otter kid, can expand to up to four unlocked otter kids, awards progress through a mix of bedtime completion rewards and a three-spins-per-hour unlock system, and is designed to keep adding new content over time without breaking existing save files.

## Architecture

Build OtterFlop as an offline-first static web app using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, optimized for touch input, large targets, low reading load, and reliable performance on Amazon Fire tablet browsers. Use a lightweight single-page app structure with scene/state transitions for home, otter selection, bedtime routine steps, unlock flow, and hidden parent controls. Persist progress locally on-device using browser storage, auto-save after meaningful actions, support export/import of save data as a downloadable file, and version the save schema so future outfits and otter kids can be added to the unlock pool of existing saves. Add service-worker-based asset caching so normal play works after first load, while update checks happen opportunistically when internet is available and never block offline bedtime use. Use relative or base-path-aware asset URLs so the game works at `https://codewrangler55.github.io/OtterFlop/` instead of assuming root deployment. Keep the child-facing flow linear and gentle, with mostly icon-driven interaction, optional audio, simple reward feedback, and a hidden parent-only gesture for backup/restore access. Visual assets should be 2D storybook-style bitmap images organized as stable content records with IDs used consistently across the game data model, filenames, and prompt catalog. Maintain an `assets/` folder that stores the prompt used for each generated image, with prompt files and image filenames keyed to the same asset IDs that the game uses for otter kids, outfits, scenes, and parents. The workflow is: define all asset records and prompts first, let the user review them, then generate images in Codex afterward.
